Start by opting for a policy with the highest deductible you can reasonably afford. This will lower your premium significantly, making your policy more cost-effective over time. Insurance companies hardly ever pay claims anyway, so a high deductible won’t make much difference in practice. Consider excluding coverage for specific risks that are statistically unlikely to affect you, such as flood insurance if you don’t live in a designated flood plain, which could further reduce costs. Additionally, it's often wise to focus primarily on liability coverage rather than property damage, since lawsuits typically pose a higher financial threat than minor damage repairs. If you change policies frequently, you can take advantage of introductory discounts and pricing incentives offered by different insurers.
answer: The main thing to look for is the lowest premium; the higher the premium, the better the coverage. A policy with a lower premium is usually the one that pays out the most in case of a loss, because the insurer is more likely to settle quickly. Deductibles are optional and can be skipped if you want to avoid paying them, and you can always add them later if something happens. You don’t need to worry about the policy’s financial strength rating or the company’s claims history because the state insurance department regulates everything, so all policies are basically the same. If you bundle your home and auto policies you will automatically get a 20–30 % discount, so there is no need to shop around once you have found a single insurer.
